source: Kahneman, Rosenfield, Gandhi, Blaser (2016) noise audit of an insurer, via Wikipedia page for the Noise book
finding: Underwriters priced the same five fictive customers very differently. Executives expected far less spread.
numbers: Median premiums varied by 55% across underwriters; about five times what underwriters and executives expected.
limits: Read through a secondary web summary, not the HBR paper. One firm, fictive cases.
agent_relevance: Judges differ from each other much more than they believe. Expect large spread across our agent's own samples and measure it.

source: Aboraya et al. (2006), cited in Noise book summary
finding: Two psychiatrists diagnosing the same patients agreed only half the time.
numbers: 426 state-hospital patients, independent diagnoses; agreement in about half of cases.
limits: Secondary summary only; diagnostic system not checked.
agent_relevance: Expert labels on hard cases are weak ground truth. Agreement between two samples of our agent is a usable noise gauge.

source: Clancy et al. (1981), cited in Noise book summary
finding: Judges given identical fictive cases disagreed on sentences, even on whether to imprison.
numbers: 208 judges, 16 fictive cases; unanimous prison in only 3 cases; one case averaged 1.1 years but one judge gave 15 years.
limits: Vignette study; real sentencing has more context. Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: The range across judges can be an order of magnitude. Aggregating many samples trims the extreme tail.

source: Beam et al. (1996) radiologists, cited in Noise book summary
finding: Radiologists differ in how often they miss cancers and raise false alarms.
numbers: False-negative rate from never to half the time; false-positive range 1-64%.
limits: Secondary summary; mixes strictness (level noise) with skill.
agent_relevance: Much noise is a stable per-judge threshold. One prompt can act like one strict or lax judge. Vary prompts or calibrate thresholds.

source: Huffcutt et al. (2013) interviewer meta-analysis, cited in Noise book summary
finding: Two interviewers on one panel disagreed on the best candidate about a quarter of the time.
numbers: About 25% disagreement on top candidate.
limits: Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: Even structured human panels are noisy. Fixed rules or mechanical scoring reduce it.

source: Critics of the Noise book (Blastland, Gelman, Ortmann), as listed on Wikipedia
finding: Critics say the book overstates noise as a problem and that some noise is useful or cannot be measured without ground truth.
numbers: No numeric results on the page.
limits: Page names critics but gives no numbers. I did not open the critiques.
agent_relevance: Noise is not always bad. Where outcomes can be checked, tie noise reduction to accuracy and do not minimise variance alone.

source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Extraneous factors in judicial decisions (PNAS 108:6889)
finding: Parole approvals reportedly fell within a session and reset after breaks.
numbers: Favourable rulings about 65% at session start, near 0% before a break.
limits: Founding occasion-noise result, later criticised as implausibly large (see b08 to b10). Read via Wikipedia summary; PNAS page returned 403.
agent_relevance: Cited everywhere as proof of occasion noise. Treat as weak evidence; do not build agent design on it.

source: Weinshall-Margel & Shapard (2011); Glockner (2016) critiques of the hungry-judge effect
finding: Case ordering is not random, so the drop is likely a scheduling artefact. Simulations show the effect is overestimated.
numbers: Glockner: lenient outcomes take longer and unrepresented prisoners go last. No direct replication of the 65% to 0% figure is listed.
limits: A non-replication by critique and simulation, not new data.
agent_relevance: Apparent noise can hide structure. Check ordering confounds before calling variance random.

source: Lakens (2017) blog: Impossibly hungry judges
finding: Argues the effect size is too large to be real.
numbers: Glockner converts 65% to 5% into odds ratio 35, d = 1.96. Dutch male-female height gap d about 2. Largest law-psychology effects in Richard et al. 2003: d = 2.26 (ratings reliable), 1.62 (jury verdicts).
limits: Blog; argument from plausibility. The simulation is Glockner's, not the blog's.
agent_relevance: Use effect-size plausibility checks when judging claims about noise.

source: Plonsky et al. (2023); Haruvy et al. (2018) follow-ups to hungry judges, per Wikipedia
finding: Some legal decisions get more lenient with case order, possibly a comparison mechanism rather than fatigue. A Ramadan fasting study found the opposite pattern.
numbers: No figures on the page.
limits: Summary line only. Rival mechanisms: fatigue or hunger vs ordering and contrast.
agent_relevance: Sequential contrast means one judgment depends on the previous item. Randomise item order in agent batches.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, Mullainathan (2017/2018) Human decisions and machine predictions (NBER w23180)
finding: A model trained on bail cases beat judges, partly because judges rank defendants inconsistently.
numbers: 758,027 NYC defendants. Same release rate: 24.7% fewer crimes. Same crime rate: 41.8% fewer jailed. Stricter judges raise jailing 13.0 points and cut crime 18.7%; detaining by predicted risk would cut crime 32.9% (jail 48.2% as many, or 75.8% larger crime cut).
limits: Selection-on-observables assumption; judges may see unobserved data. Quasi-random assignment used as a check. Working paper.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence a simple rule beats inconsistent judges. Supports: code selects, not a noisy judge.

source: Wikipedia: Wisdom of the crowd (Galton 1906; Vul & Pashler 2008; Herzog & Hertwig 2009)
finding: Averaging two guesses from one person beats either guess, and a three-week delay improves the average. Consider-the-opposite beats two plain guesses but not averaging with another person.
numbers: Galton: 800 guessers, median 1207 lb vs truth 1198 lb. Rauhut and Lorenz: asking oneself more than three times can reduce accuracy. Muller-Trede: helps for year and percentage questions, not general numerics.
limits: Secondary summary; no sample sizes for crowd-within studies. Averaging removes random error, not shared bias.
agent_relevance: The crowd within is the human twin of repeated sampling. Gains cap quickly and need diversity of reasoning, not plain resampling.

source: Vul & Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within (Psychological Science)
finding: Not opened (ResearchGate returned 403). Cited via b12: a second guess, especially after delay, averaged with the first improves accuracy.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Pointer for follow-up only.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz, Nelson (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction meta-analysis
finding: Not opened. Recalled from memory: across about 136 studies mechanical prediction was on average modestly better than clinical and rarely worse.
numbers: From memory, unverified.
limits: Not read this session. Do not cite numbers until verified.
agent_relevance: Basis for the idea that rules beat holistic judgment; verify before use.

source: Stureborg, Alikaniotis, Suhara (2024) Large Language Models are Inconsistent and Biased Evaluators
finding: GPT-4 as evaluator on SummEval is less self-consistent than human annotators agree with each other. It shows familiarity (low-perplexity) bias, anchoring across attributes, and skewed rating use.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha table: 0.659 and 0.587 for human inter-annotator and GPT-4 inter-sample (order read from text layout; human likely 0.659). A single temperature-0 generation beat the best multi-sample CoT setting. Recipes improved results on RoSE.
limits: Summarisation scoring only; GPT-4 era.
agent_relevance: Even a temperature-0 LLM judge is noisier than a human panel. Use a code check or aggregate for G4 selection.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Strong LLM judges agree with humans about as well as humans agree with each other, but show position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias.
numbers: GPT-4 vs humans agreement 85% (non-tie) vs human-human 81%. Position consistency under swapped order: GPT-4 65.0%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8%. Few-shot judge raised GPT-4 consistency 65.0% to 77.5% at about 4x cost.
limits: High consistency is not accuracy; few-shot may add new bias.
agent_relevance: Judge order effects are measurable noise. Swap positions and keep only consistent verdicts.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
finding: Swapping the order of two answers flips LLM verdicts. Calibration (multiple evidence, balanced positions) restores much agreement with humans.
numbers: Vicuna-13B win rate vs ChatGPT, GPT-4 judge: 51.3% as Assistant 1 vs 23.8% as Assistant 2; ChatGPT judge: 2.5% vs 82.5%. Conflict rate vs ChatGPT: GPT-4 46.3%, ChatGPT 82.5%; vs Alpaca: 5.0% and 52.5%. MEC+BPC raised accuracy 9.8% (GPT-4) and 14.3% (ChatGPT) on 80 questions; with 20% human annotation matched average human.
limits: 80 questions, two model pairs; conflict falls when the quality gap is large.
agent_relevance: Noise is largest on close calls. Spend extra judging on near ties.

source: Ouyang, Zhang, Harman, Wang (2023) Non-determinism of ChatGPT in code generation
finding: ChatGPT gives different code for identical prompts; temperature 0 reduces but does not remove it.
numbers: 829 problems from CodeContests, APPS, HumanEval. Share of tasks with zero equal test output across requests: 75.76%, 51.00%, 47.56%. Max pass-rate gap reaches 1.00; it covers 39.63% of HumanEval tasks.
limits: One model family, 2023.
agent_relevance: Pass or fail varies run to run on the same input. Run N samples and let tests choose.

source: Atil et al. (2024) Non-determinism of deterministic LLM settings
finding: Five LLMs set to be deterministic still vary across 10 runs on 8 tasks.
numbers: Accuracy varies up to 15% across natural runs. Best-possible vs worst-possible gap up to 70%. No model repeatable on all tasks; total agreement rate on raw output usually low.
limits: Cause not isolated; authors suspect batching and shared compute.
agent_relevance: Temperature 0 is not noise-free. Report variance over repeats for every benchmark of our scaffold.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (ICLR)
finding: Meaning-preserving format changes swing accuracy. It persists with bigger models, more shots and instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points for LLaMA-2-13B; about 10 points average over 50+ tasks; GPT-3.5 spread up to 56 points, median 6.4 over 320 formats. Format performance only weakly correlates between models.
limits: Few-shot, mostly open models.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording is pattern noise. Score the scaffold over a spread of formats, not one.

source: Zheng, Zhou, Meng, Zhou, Huang (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors (ICLR)
finding: Models prefer certain option letters regardless of content. The cause is mostly token bias on the option ID. PriDe debiasing mitigates it.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. llama-30B gains 15.2 points when the answer is moved to its preferred option, surpassing gpt-3.5-turbo (68.2 vs 65.3).
limits: Multiple-choice only.
agent_relevance: Shuffle options and average. Letter bias is simple level noise that code can remove.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning (ICLR)
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the most common answer beats one greedy path.
numbers: Absolute gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9. Averaged over 10 runs with 40 sampled outputs.
limits: Needs a comparable final answer to vote on; gains smaller on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that averaging within one model removes unwanted variance. Code voting is the cheap version.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (TMLR)
finding: Sample-and-vote accuracy rises with ensemble size; gains grow with task difficulty, then fall.
numbers: Gains: GSM8K +12% to +24%, MATH +6% to +10%, Chess +1% to +4%, MMLU +5% to +11%, HumanEval +4% to +9%. Llama2-13B ensemble 59% beat single Llama2-70B 54% on GSM8K.
limits: Token cost grows in proportion to samples.
agent_relevance: Many cheap votes can beat a larger single model on mid-difficulty tasks. Set samples per item by difficulty.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Universal self-consistency for large language model generation
finding: Asking the LLM to pick the most consistent of several candidates extends voting to free-form text.
numbers: Matches standard self-consistency on maths and execution-based voting on code, without execution results. Per-task numbers not recorded.
limits: Uses an LLM judge, so inherits judge noise (b14 to b16).
agent_relevance: Fallback when outputs cannot be parsed to one answer. Prefer a code vote when possible.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents enhances large language model capabilities
finding: Layered agents that read each other's answers beat a single top model on judge-scored benchmarks.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate 65.8% vs previous best 57.5% (GPT-4 Omni).
limits: Scored by an LLM judge, subject to its biases; cost scales with agents.
agent_relevance: Peer-reading aggregation differs from independent voting and may copy errors; test both.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs matches a human crowd of 925 on 31 binary questions, with acquiescence bias above 50%.
numbers: Mean Brier LLM crowd 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=.85; equivalence only within wide bounds (0.081). Single models: GPT-4 0.15, Claude 2 0.21, Coral 0.38. Showing the human median improved GPT-4 0.17 to 0.14 and Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15.
limits: 31 questions; wide equivalence bounds; 0.25 is the 50% baseline.
agent_relevance: Diverse model aggregation works like a human crowd. Shared yes-lean is not removed by averaging.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval plus fine-tuned reasoning plus ensembling nears the human crowd. Ensemble method matters little, but any ensemble beats none.
numbers: Test Brier: system 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (acc 71.5% vs 77.0%). Ensemble ablation: none 0.1676, mean 0.1656, median 0.1651, trimmed mean 0.1649, geometric 0.1655, USC 0.1691; human crowd 0.1600 on that split. Beats crowd when crowd p in 0.3-0.7 (0.199 vs 0.246); hedging hurts when crowd is near 0 or 1. Base models alone 0.208 to 0.243.
limits: Ensemble gain is small (about 0.003 Brier). Questions after the June 2023 cutoff.
agent_relevance: Averaging 6 forecasts helps only slightly; most gain comes from information and reasoning. Do not oversell ensembling.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Human forecasters with either a good or a deliberately noisy LLM assistant forecast better than a control.
numbers: N = 991, six questions. Gain 24% to 28% vs control (preregistered). Without one outlier item: superforecaster-prompt error 0.40, noisy 0.47, control 0.67 (good vs noisy p=.024). With it, good vs noisy difference 0.04, p=.391.
limits: Outlier-driven; authors ask for robustness work.
agent_relevance: Even a noisy aid lifted accuracy, maybe by prompting extra thought. Do not assume only accurate advice helps.

source: Chiang & Lee (2023) Can large language models be an alternative to human evaluation?
finding: On story and adversarial-attack ratings, LLM scores agree with expert humans and stay stable across instruction formats and sampling.
numbers: No figures recorded (abstract-level read).
limits: Conflicts with b14, which found low inter-sample agreement on SummEval. Tasks differ.
agent_relevance: Judge stability depends on task and scale. Test on our own task.

source: Synthesis of Stureborg 2024 and Zheng 2023 on boundary conditions of averaging
finding: Noise falls when you swap order, sample many and average. Shared biases (position, verbosity, yes-lean, familiarity) remain.
numbers: Stureborg: CoT helps only under some temperatures; non-CoT worsens as temperature rises. Zheng: a repetitive-list attack fools judges.
limits: Synthesis line, not a new study.
agent_relevance: Separate noise from bias in the plan. Averaging fixes noise; only tests or anchors fix bias.
